vignette:
Arthur was 72 when he first sought help, the weight of decades of unaddressed trauma finally pressing down with an unbearable force. Many years ago, he had endured a period of unspeakable torture, an experience that had stripped him of his autonomy and forced him into actions that, in his eyes, irrevocably stained his character. He had been held captive, interrogated, and subjected to abuses that left him profoundly changed, particularly the memory of having to betray others under duress. This profound violation of his core self had led him to believe, with a deep, aching certainty, that he had acted in ways that went against who he truly was, a crushing burden he carried silently.

In the years that followed, this internal conviction that he had violated his values began to shape his daily life in subtle yet pervasive ways. He found himself constantly monitoring his own thoughts for any signs of weakness, any hint that he might truly be "going crazy" from the strain. He tried hard not to think about the trauma, pushing away the images and feelings whenever they arose, convinced that dwelling on them would only confirm his deepest fears about his own unraveling. This suppression, however, often brought the memories back with greater intensity, leaving him feeling even more isolated and set apart from others, convinced no one could ever understand the darkness within him.

His professional life as a software engineer, often demanding long hours and intense focus, became a stage for his growing vigilance. At his downtown office, Arthur found himself studying people’s faces and body language, searching for any flicker of malevolence, any subtle sign that they might pose a threat. This constant, exhausting assessment of others, a direct consequence of his past, led him to the disheartening conclusion that he had lost faith in people, seeing them as inherently untrustworthy, which in turn deepened his profound sense of isolation. When he returned home, the quiet of his apartment became another source of distress. He would repeatedly check that doors and windows were locked, sometimes multiple times, a ritual born from a pervasive sense of impending danger. This difficulty falling asleep because he needed to stay alert, a relentless sleep vigilance, further eroded his well-being, leaving him perpetually exhausted.

The unrelenting sense of threat, whether real or perceived, significantly influenced his daily routines. His pervasive hypervigilance meant he couldn't relax, driving him to avoid being alone in a room or building whenever possible. He’d often linger at work until the last colleague left, or find excuses to visit a busy coffee shop rather than sit in his quiet apartment. This strategy, intended to keep him safe, paradoxically reinforced his belief that he was fundamentally isolated and that the world was a dangerous place where he couldn't trust anyone, including himself. The attempts to suppress thoughts about the trauma, rather than offering relief, often backfired, making the memories more intrusive and leading him to constantly monitor his own thoughts for signs of "going crazy," which only strengthened his conviction that he was fundamentally isolated and set apart from others.

Over the decades, Arthur’s world had shrunk. His lost faith in people, coupled with the profound feeling that he had violated his own values, made him withdraw from social connections, preferring the predictable logic of code to the unpredictable nature of human interaction. The constant monitoring of his thoughts and the relentless attempts to suppress the trauma, while meant to protect him, only tightened the grip of his negative appraisals, locking him into a cycle of self-blame and detachment. He found himself increasingly unable to concentrate on complex projects at work, the exhaustion from his sleep vigilance making sharp focus impossible. It was this growing professional impairment, coupled with the crushing weight of his isolation and the fear that he was truly losing his mind, that finally prompted Arthur to seek help, hoping to find some way to reconcile with the man he had become, and the man he believed he had lost.
